question.problem: A particle $P$ moves along the $x$-axis in the direction of increasing $x$ where $x\ge 0.$ When the displacement of $P$ from the origin is $x\,m,$ the velocity is $v\,m/s,$ and the acceleration is $k(6-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ where $k$ is a positive constant. If $P$ has velocity $v=2\,m/s$ at the origin and has velocity $v=2\sqrt{11}\,m/s$ when its displacement is $2\,m,$ find the maximum velocity of the particle.
question.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14164351/assets/a8ff5e02237554d0f7107168f287adbe1834c4dd7ad965163531f5a23412a4fc.png)

The extrema of the velocity occur at the critical points of $v.$ Since the acceleration of the particle $P$ is $k(6-x)\,{m/s}^{2},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=k(6-x).
$$

To find the moments where $v$ is a maximum, we need to solve $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ and test each solution using the first derivative test.

Solving $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=0$ gives

$$
\begin{aligned}k(6-x) & =0 \\ 6-x & =0 \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the extremum of the velocity function occurs when $x=6\,m.$

We now test the extreme value using the first derivative test. We summarize the necessary information in a table, shown below.

| $x$ | $(0,6)$ | $6$ | $(6,\infty )$ |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Test Point | $5$ |  | $7$ |
| $\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}$ | $k>0$ | $0$ | $-k<0$ |
| $v$ | $↗$ | max | $↘$ |

We conclude that the velocity is maximized when $x=6\,m.$

Next, using the fact that

$$
\frac{\text{d}v}{\text{d}t}=\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}),
$$

we can rewrite our initial equation as

$$
\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})=k(6-x).
$$

Integrating both sides of the above equation with respect to $x,$ we have

$$
\int \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2})\text{d}x=\int k(6-x)\,\text{d}x
$$

which gives the general solution

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C.
$$

Now, since $v=2\,m/s$ when $x=0\,m,$ we can find the value of the constant $C,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+C \\ \frac{1}{2}(2)^{2} & =k(6(0)-\frac{1}{2}(0)^{2})+C \\ C & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}=k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2.
$$

Also, since $v=2\sqrt{11}\,m/s$ when $x=2\,m,$ we can find the value of the positive constant $k,$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =k(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}(2\sqrt{11})^{2} & =k(6(2)-\frac{1}{2}{(2)}^{2})+2 \\ 22 & =10k+2 \\ 10k & =20 \\ k & =2\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =2(6x-\frac{1}{2}{x}^{2})+2 \\ \frac{1}{2}{v}^{2} & =12x-{x}^{2}+2 \\ {v}^{2} & =24x-2{x}^{2}+4 \\ v & =\pm \sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+24x+4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the particle is moving in the direction of increasing $x,$ we have that $v(x)>0,$ so we can disregard the negative square root. Therefore,

$$
v(x)=\sqrt{-2{x}^{2}+24x+4}.
$$

Finally, we calculate the maximum velocity:

$$
{v}_{max}=v(6)=\sqrt{-2(6)^{2}+24(6)+4}=2\sqrt{19}\,m/s
$$
